title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6734 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: HBM explained: the AI memory behind SK Hynix's record profits and rising chip prices
body: HBM helps explain why the memory upcycle has been so strong. Because it absorbs production capacity, AI demand lifts prices across the whole DRAM market, not just at the high end, which supports earnings at SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron and weighs on margins for PC, phone and server makers that buy memory. The concentration of supply makes the Kospi and the wider Korean market unusually sensitive to AI spending, and changes in HBM market share between SK Hynix and Samsung can move both stocks sharply. The main risk is the cycle turning: if new capacity and three-way competition in HBM4 catch up with demand, pricing power could fade quickly, as it has in past memory cycles. --- Earlier, stunning results: SK Hynix Q3 operating profit beats at 83tn won, unveils 100tn won shareholder payout plan --- HBM is the memory that keeps AI chips fed with data, and because it eats so much production capacity, it is pushing up prices for nearly every memory chip in the world. Summary: HBM stacks thin DRAM dies vertically and places them right next to the processor, delivering much higher bandwidth with less power. AI chips are often limited by how fast they can be fed data, so every leading AI accelerator, including Nvidia's GPUs, uses HBM. HBM uses around three times the wafer capacity per bit of standard DRAM, by industry estimates, so shifting production to it squeezes supply of ordinary memory and lifts prices. Only SK Hynix, Samsung and Micron make it at scale.

title: Bessent says SEC and CFTC can fill the Clarity Act gap, but agency rules come with an expiry risk
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Washington can still deliver crypto rules without Congress. Speaking at Ripple's Swell conference, he said the Senate's failure to pass the Clarity Act was disappointing, but that Treasury would use its convening power to push a regulatory framework forward through agency action with the SEC and CFTC. The catch for investors is durability: rules written by regulators can be rewritten by the next set of regulators. What happened Bessent described the SEC and CFTC as "great partners" in the effort. He also raised debanking, the practice of financial institutions cutting off services to crypto businesses, sometimes allegedly under regulatory pressure. He said the Clarity Act could have prevented a repeat of that, but that regulatory best practices and protections can still reduce the risk. He also argued that stablecoins will lift demand for the US dollar and Treasuries, making them an important funding source for the government. The backdrop is the Senate vote six weeks ago. The Clarity Act failed to advance on September 15 on a 49-50 vote, 11 short of the 60 needed. Because the vote was procedural, the bill was never debated or amended. The two disputes that sank it were ethics rules covering officials' digital asset holdings and whether stablecoin issuers can offer yield or rewards. Why it matters The bill would have settled the question that has dogged US crypto for years: which regulator is responsible for which tokens.

title: UBS sees Brent near $110 by year-end, lifts 2027 forecasts on freight and supply risks
body: UBS is arguing that the oil market's tightness has moved from production to logistics. Even with Gulf flows close to pre-conflict levels, shipping attacks and scarce tankers keep delivered crude expensive, which means a supply recovery alone may not bring prices down much. With strategic reserve releases largely done and Chinese buying back, the market has lost two of its main shock absorbers, leaving it more exposed to any new disruption around Hormuz. Higher-for-longer oil also keeps inflation pressure in play ahead of the Fed decision, adding to the case for further tightening and weighing on rate-sensitive assets. Freight-sensitive refiners and importers in Asia are the most exposed to the shift from barrel scarcity to shipping scarcity. --- Earlier: Oil: Private survey of inventory shows a headline crude oil draw vs build expected --- Gulf oil is flowing again, but UBS says record attacks on shipping, drained inventories and returning Chinese demand mean the barrels are getting more expensive to move, keeping Brent elevated well into 2027. Summary: UBS expects Brent to hold near $110 by year-end and raised its 2027 forecasts: March to $95 from $90, June to $90 from $85 and September to $85 from $80. Global inventories have fallen sharply and pledged strategic reserve releases are largely complete, which UBS says should support prices.

body: Wall Street enjoyed a bit of a breather in overnight trading, as the S&P 500 gained by 0.6% and Nasdaq closed higher by 1.2%. It's a welcome relief after drop in the past two weeks as tech shares bounced back, but there are still plenty of reasons for investors to be nervous in trading this week. For one, the rebound overnight was not all too convincing once we start to dig a little deeper beneath the surface. It was largely driven by big tech names with most of the stocks in the S&P 500 actually closing lower. That's not a good signal on market breadth now, is it? And with the Fed decision coming up later today, followed by earnings from Microsoft and Alphabet after the closing bell, there's still quite a lot that could go wrong. Now, the Fed is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged. So, I don't see the decision itself being much of a surprise. All eyes will be on Fed chair Warsh's press conference as markets will be listening closely for any signals on December, particularly with Treasury yields still hovering near 5%. With that in mind, any suggestion that policymakers are becoming even more uncomfortable with the inflation outlook could easily put another dent in risk sentiment. And that will be especially relevant for tech stocks, where higher borrowing costs and lofty valuations are already making investors question just how much optimism is justified.

title: European markets brace for Fed decision as hot Australia CPI, RBNZ surprise and oil rally stir nerves
body: It has been quite an eventful start to the day so far as the central bank bonanza rolls into town. That is putting inflation back in the spotlight with there already being plenty to digest before European traders get to their desks and before we even get to the main events later today. To start with, we saw Australia's latest CPI report came in hotter than expected with trimmed mean inflation rising to 3.7%. That's not a good look and RBA governor Bullock was quick to respond in warning that inflation remains "far too high". The numbers certainly strengthen the argument for another rate hike, with Bullock's response underscoring the narrative that the central bank is facing an increasingly uncomfortable inflation outlook. As such, that is now seeing markets step up their pricing for the next RBA meeting on 3 November, with traders pricing in roughly 76% odds of a 25 bps rate hike. Meanwhile, the RBNZ delivered arguably the bigger surprise of the session after keeping its official cash rate unchanged at 2.75% in a narrow 4-3 vote. Markets had been expecting a 25 bps rate hike today, so the decision has definitely caught traders off guard and sent the kiwi sharply lower. NZD/USD is down 1.1% to 0.5615 on the day currently. Having said that, the central bank hasn't abandoned its tightening bias altogether as the minority continued to take on a more hawkish stance.

title: Topix explained: why Japan's biggest-ever index overhaul will cull 683 stocks by 2028
body: The immediate effect comes at Thursday's close, when around $60 billion of passive trades is expected to cause sharp, short-lived price swings and heavy volume in affected stocks. That can briefly distort the Topix and individual names, which is why hedge funds have been positioning in advance. Over time, the quarterly weight cuts create steady selling pressure on smaller, less liquid companies and support larger stocks such as Kioxia. That may widen the gap between Japanese large caps and small caps. The 2027 re-evaluation gives companies a reason to improve liquidity and free float, which could encourage more unwinding of cross-shareholdings and buybacks. That fits the governance push foreign investors have rewarded. Watch for a temporary gap between the Topix and the Nikkei 225, which isn't affected. --- Japan is turning its sprawling Topix into a leaner, more investable benchmark, and with about ¥166 trillion tracking it, the reshuffle starts with a $60 billion trade on Thursday and keeps going for two years. Summary: The Topix's largest-ever overhaul takes effect on October 30, with about $60 billion of passive trading expected at Thursday's close, the Japan Times reported. 683 companies that failed new liquidity and free-float tests will be phased out, with their weights cut in eight quarterly steps from January 2027 to zero in October 2028. Companies that meet the criteria at an October 2027 re-evaluation stop being cut and remain in the index.

title: RBNZ's Breman: more hikes likely at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory
body: Breman's guidance partly reverses the dovish read of the hold. Signalling likely hikes at coming meetings, possibly into restrictive territory, should push December pricing back up, support front-end yields and help the New Zealand dollar recover some of its losses. Her explicit worry about a weak currency feeding imported inflation acts as a soft floor for the kiwi, since further falls make a hike more likely. Oil is the main swing factor: fuel is already lifting inflation toward 4.4%, so higher crude, especially if a US strike on Iran escalates after the midterms, would make a December hike much more likely. The guidance also narrows the policy gap with the RBA, which may cap AUD/NZD after this morning's divergence. --- The RBNZ held, then Breman spent the press conference telling markets not to read too much into it: more hikes are likely, and they may go further than planned. Summary: RBNZ Governor Anna Breman said further rate increases are likely at coming meetings, and tightening might be needed even into restrictive territory. The committee agreed tighter policy is likely, conditional on the economy, and discussed whether rates could rise further than its projected OCR path. Breman said the committee is concerned that a sustained fall in the NZ dollar could add to imported inflation. She said the decision was based on the economic outlook, though the committee did look at market pricing, and that wage growth remains below levels consistent with the inflation target.

title: US warns Gulf allies of possible short, intense Iran campaign after midterms: WSJ
body: This is a direct upside risk for oil. A renewed US campaign against Iran would revive the threat of Iranian retaliation against Gulf energy facilities, shipping and infrastructure, which Iran has already shown it is willing to target. With Brent already around $115, the Houthi refinery claim adding to supply nerves and OPEC+ unlikely to add barrels on Sunday, a risk premium could build in the days before the November 3 midterms. Freight and insurance costs for Gulf shipping are also exposed. The inflation consequences extend well beyond the region: higher crude would add to the pressure that the RBA flagged today and complicate Fed policy. Safe-haven flows into the dollar are possible. Gold has tended to fall on escalation as rate expectations rise. -- Washington is quietly telling Gulf allies to brace for a post-midterms strike on Iran, and with Tehran promising to hit back at energy targets, oil markets have six days to price the risk. Summary: The US told several Gulf Arab states to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign against Iran after the November 3 midterms, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported. Trump is leaning toward a large strike on Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites but has not decided, according to people familiar with his thinking. The US is moving a Patriot system to the region, restocking munitions and adding a carrier strike group to roughly 20 warships already deployed. Israel has also prepared strike plans.

title: Oil edges higher after Houthis claim missile strike on Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery
body: The key issue for oil is whether the Houthi claim turns into confirmed lost supply. For now, the move reflects headline risk on a refinery Saudi Arabia hasn't confirmed was hit, so prices are exposed to a reversal if the damage proves limited, or a sharper rally if refining capacity is knocked out. A hit to a facility of this size would matter more for refined products such as diesel than for crude, which fits the shipping and refining strains UBS and the RBNZ flagged this week. OPEC+ holding steady on Sunday, with most core members already below target, offers little cushion if supply is disrupted. Higher crude also feeds straight into the inflation concerns voiced today by RBA Governor Bullock (here and again here). Oil clawed back some of Tuesday's losses on a Houthi claim of a strike on Saudi Arabia's biggest refinery, but until Riyadh confirms the damage, the market is pricing risk, not lost barrels. Summary: Brent rose around 1.3% to around $115 and WTI around 1.2% to around $101 as of 01:40 GMT, according to Reuters. Yemen's Houthis said they struck Saudi Arabia's largest refinery, a 550,000 bpd facility. Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the strike. Reuters said the attack renewed concerns about Middle East supply risks. Prices had fallen nearly $2 on Tuesday as regional talks eased worries. A Reuters poll pointed to a build of about 15,000 barrels in US crude inventories for the week ended October 23.

title: RBA's Bullock: Inflation is far too high
body: By saying it is hard to completely look through supply shocks, Bullock signalled that the RBA is less willing to ignore the energy-driven jump in prices than the RBNZ was earlier. Any further rise in crude therefore adds directly to the case for an RBA hike. Her blunt language (more here earlier), together with firmer core inflation and her view that demand still exceeds supply, supports pricing for a move on November 2 and 3, and backs the Australian dollar and front-end yields. The contrast with the RBNZ's hold sharpens the policy divergence, which favours AUD/NZD. Bullock's refusal to give guidance leaves some uncertainty, but the overall tone tilts clearly hawkish. --- Bullock didn't pre-announce a hike, but "far too high" and "difficult to look through supply shocks" are about as close as a central banker gets without saying it. Summary: RBA Governor Michele Bullock said inflation is far too high, in Senate committee testimony after the Q3 CPI release. She said the data was consistent with upside inflation risks and that it is difficult to completely look through supply shocks. Bullock said domestic demand is still higher than domestic supply, but declined to give guidance on the November 2 and 3 Board decision. Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser said the CPI was in line with expectations but too high. Assistant Governor Sarah Hunter said it was stronger than the RBA expected in August. Hunter said she does not expect a recession in Australia.

body: Both economies face the same fuel shock, but Bullock treats it as a reason for concern, while the RBNZ majority is betting weak demand will contain it. That difference in reaction is what drives the divergence. A widening gap in expected rates generally supports AUD/NZD, and a hike from the RBA next week, with the RBNZ waiting until December, would extend it. The main risk to the move is the RBNZ's 4-3 split: hawkish signals from Breman at the press conference, or a firm December hike signal, could pull the cross back quickly. A softer tone from the RBA next week would do the same. Further gains in crude would test both banks, but the RBA currently looks the more willing to respond. --- Earlier: RBNZ holds OCR at 2.75% in surprise 4-3 vote, says tighter policy still likely Australia trimmed mean CPI rises to 3.7%, above forecasts, as RBA hike case firms RBA's Bullock: oil shock means inflation above August forecasts, Board meets next week --- Within 90 minutes, Australia signalled it may need to tighten further and New Zealand decided to wait, and AUD/NZD is where that divergence shows up. title: RBNZ holds OCR at 2.75% in surprise 4-3 vote, says tighter policy still likely
body: Oil sits at the centre of the call: the RBNZ expects fuel to lift inflation to 4.4% in the December quarter, but the majority chose to look through the direct effects for now, betting that weak demand will limit pass-through. With a hike close to fully priced, the hold is likely to hit the New Zealand dollar and pull front-end yields lower. The 4-3 split and the guidance that tighter policy is still likely should limit how far December pricing unwinds. Policy divergence is now sharp. Hotter Australian core inflation this morning and a hawkish Bullock contrast with a cautious RBNZ, which points to upside for AUD/NZD into the RBA meeting on November 2 and 3. The RBNZ's warning about opaque AI financing and an abrupt global downturn adds a dovish tail risk that markets had largely ignored. --- Background: All 5 major NZ banks expect RBNZ to hike to 3% today, but split on how far rates will go Preview: RBNZ set to lift OCR to 3% ahead of election as oil and weak kiwi fuel inflation NZIER Shadow Board majority backs 25bp RBNZ hike to 3% as oil and weaker kiwi bite --- The RBNZ blinked: with a hike almost fully priced, four of seven members chose to wait, betting that weak demand will contain the fuel shock, while keeping December firmly in play. Summary: The RBNZ held the OCR at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote. Breman, Hansen, Williams and Gai voted to hold, while Gourley, Conway and Silk voted for a hike to 3%.

title: UK budget: Growth forecasts cut as Healey unveils £15 billion fiscal buffer
body: The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) lowered its near-term growth forecasts but the government still expects to meet its fiscal rules, with £15 billion of headroom at the end of the forecast period. The headline growth revisions: 2026 GDP: 1.2% vs 1.1% in March 2027 GDP: 1.0% vs 1.6% in March 2028 GDP: 1.6% vs 1.6% in March 2029 GDP: 1.8% vs 1.5% in March 2030 GDP: 1.7% vs 1.5% in March 2031 GDP: 1.6% The sharp downgrade to 2027 is the standout number, with growth now expected at just 1.0%. The revisions further out are more constructive but that's the usual tactic. On the fiscal side, the numbers show a deterioration in the debt outlook: 2026/27 public sector net financial liabilities: 83.2% of GDP vs 82.6% previously 2027/28: 83.8% vs 82.9% 2028/29: 83.8% vs 82.9% 2029/30: 83.1% vs 82.2% 2030/31: 82.3% vs 81.1% 2031/32: 81.7% The OBR also forecasts a budget deficit of 4.2% of GDP this year, narrowing to 3.4% next year. Public sector net borrowing is projected at 1.8% of GDP in 2030/31, compared with 1.6% in the March forecast. Healey said the government will spend an additional £14 billion on debt interest this year, underscoring the damage from higher global borrowing costs. The chancellor ruled out broad-based tax increases and deep cuts to public services, while pledging to maintain the government's fiscal rules. Some of the remaining fiscal headroom will be used to absorb the impact of the Iran war.

title: US Wholesale inventories 0.6% vs 0.5% estimate
body: Wholesale inventories: +0.6% MoM. Prior +0.5%, unrevised. Retail inventories: +0.3% MoM. Prior revised to +0.3% from +0.2%. Wholesale inventories: $1,011.5 billion, up 7.4% YoY. Retail inventories: $885.3 billion, up 4.8% YoY. US wholesale inventories rose 0.6% in September, following a 0.5% increase in August, according to the Census Bureau's advance estimates. Retail inventories increased 0.3%, matching August's upwardly revised gain. Both wholesale and retail inventories remained above year-earlier levels. The figures are adjusted for seasonal variations and trading day differences, but not for price changes. Quick analysis: Wholesale stockbuilding picked up, while retail inventory growth held steady. Inventories can support gross domestic product (GDP) growth when the pace of accumulation accelerates, but rising stocks can reflect either preparation for stronger sales or unsold goods. Sales data and inflation-adjusted quarterly figures are needed to judge the impact. On their own, these readings offer limited direction for Federal Reserve policy, Treasury yields or the dollar. What this report measures: Advance inventory estimates track the value of goods held by wholesalers and retailers at month-end. These preliminary figures are subject to revision and are not adjusted for inflation. Traders monitor inventories for clues about demand, business activity and their contribution to GDP. This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

title: US September advance goods trade balance -134.9 billion vs -130.2 billion expected
body: Prior was -132.6 These are the two worst back-to-back months since just before Liberation Day, when goods were flooding into the US to try to front-run Trump's tariffs. Excluding Jan-Mar 2025, it's the worst two-month period ever. Needless to say, tariffs aren't working. For background, the advance goods trade balance is part of the Census Bureau's Advance Economic Indicators report, released at 8:30 am ET roughly four weeks after the reference month ends. The same release includes advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories, making it one of the more useful early inputs for tracking GDP. The headline figure is the US deficit in goods trade, the difference between the value of goods exported and imported. It's broken down by end-use category: foods, feeds and beverages; industrial supplies and materials; capital goods; automotive vehicles and parts; consumer goods; and other goods. The figures are seasonally adjusted and in nominal dollars, on a Census basis. The advance report covers goods only. Services trade, where the US runs a surplus, is added in the full international trade report from the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis, published about a week later. That full report also includes country-level detail and revisions to the advance goods figures. The data matter mainly for GDP. Net exports are a component of growth, and a wider goods deficit generally subtracts from GDP while a narrower one adds to it.

title: Heads up: UK autumn budget puts Healey to the test as gilt markets await fiscal reassurance
body: UK chancellor Healey has a rather unenviable task at hand today. He is expected to deliver a budget that keeps households happy, businesses afloat, and bond investors calm. All while trying to convince everyone that the government isn't running short of money. Well, good luck with that. It is definitely quite the juggling act for his first autumn budget. And with borrowing costs still elevated and fiscal headroom shrinking, there's not exactly much room for him to get creative. So, what goodies can Healey realistically pull out of the bag today? And perhaps more importantly for markets, it is the question of who's going to end up paying for them? Here are some of the key measures to watch out for: Bank tax hike: A potential reversal of the bank surcharge cut from 8% to 3%, which could raise over £2 billion annually Online marketplace taxes: Requiring platforms like Amazon and eBay to collect VAT from more UK sellers, potentially raising £1 billion to fund business rates relief for smaller shops Energy bill relief: Over £1 billion in support for poorer households, including a possible £100 increase to the existing £150 Warm Home Discount Fuel duty freeze: Another extension looks likely, although that could cost the Treasury up to £2.7 billion annually Housing support: A proposed 20% equity loan for first-time buyers purchasing new-build homes, requiring deposits of just 2.5% Now, that is quite the shopping list for someone with limited fiscal room to work with.

title: Macro pulse: Has the RBNZ shock exposed a bigger problem with central bank rate pricing?
body: The central bank bonanza definitely kicked off with a bang today. While markets have been talking about the Fed all week, the RBNZ offered traders a bit of a reality check earlier today to not take anything for granted. Even with traders pricing in a roughly 90% chance of a 25 bps rate hike, the central bank instead held rates at 2.75% in a close 4-3 vote. The surprise in terms of market reaction is captured by the kiwi, with NZD/USD down 1.3% to 0.5605 today. But is there a broader lesson that goes beyond what we have seen so far? For the better part of the last decade, traders have grown accustomed to central banks offering plenty of forward guidance and holding their hands through major policy decisions. Central bankers would more or less signal their next move well in advance, giving traders a relatively clear path to follow in the lead up to the upcoming meeting. Now, that kind of luxury appears to be slowly disappearing. The fact of the matter is that central banks are having to deal with a very difficult balancing act at the moment. Inflation pressures remain stubborn and higher borrowing costs as well as mounting fiscal pressures are taking a toll on growth conditions, making it tough for central banks to commit to a particular policy path. In looking at the RBNZ today, policymakers weren't convinced that another rate hike was necessary just yet even with inflation running at 3.7% and projected to rise to 4.4% in the final quarter of the year.

title: Germany's trade struggles with China set to put Asia-Pacific deficit on course for record high
body: For quite some time now, Germany's export struggles are hardly anything new. A lot of that comes down to push to diversify away from China in recent times but Beijing's own ambitions to become more self-sufficient haven't exactly helped matters either. That has slowly exerted a toll on Europe's largest economy, especially when you consider how much Germany's industrial sector has relied on Chinese demand over the years. And a new report from Germany Trade & Invest (GTAI) today is offering another warning of the challenges to come, with the report projecting that Germany is set to post a record trade deficit of nearly €146 billion with Asia-Pacific in 2026. The detailed projection shows that exports to the region are expected to decline by 3.2% to €185.3 billion. Meanwhile, imports are forecast to rise by 6.4% to €330.9 billion. But perhaps the most telling detail is that excluding China, Germany's trade deficit with Asia-Pacific would narrow to just under €35 billion. Yowza. Just by that alone, you can see where the biggest problem lies for Germany. For years, German manufacturers have enjoyed a strong position in China - especially when it came to automobiles and machinery. However, those days look to be over as Chinese manufacturers have stepped up to close the gap, and in some areas, even move ahead of their German counterparts. There's no better example to that than the auto industry.
